title: US Supreme Court denies Christa Pike's last-ditch bid to halt execution
description: Slemmer's murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with s
body: Slemmer's murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself. She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.Her attorneys have argued that "an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain" and that Pike was too young at the time of the murder to be sentenced to death for it. At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.She is due to be executed at 11:00 EDT (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Additional reporting from Sareen Habeshian.Clarification 29 September: This article originally referred to a pentagram as "a symbol of Satanic ritual". We have amended the wording to make clear that the symbol in question was an inverted pentagram and to clarify that such symbols are associated with some satanic groups. The article has been updated accordingly.

schema.headline: US Supreme Court denies Christa Pike's last-ditch bid to halt execution

title: More than 400 detained as France student protests escalate
description: "We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old female student told the AFP news agency. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason. We'r
body: "We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old female student told the AFP news agency. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason. We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked."Taking to X, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said students have the right to protest, but condemned reports of violence as "indefensible".Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told BFMTV 440 people were detained, adding: "We don't have the final tally yet, but I'm told two thirds led to police custody."French media reported that protesters hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas. Speaking to AFP, Ryad Rani, president of Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force.When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has been criticised by several French politicians, Nuñez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner".Writing on social media on Tuesday evening, education minister Geffray said: "The right to demonstrate is a fundamental freedom that cannot serve as an excuse for such actions."To legitimise them or, in this context, to call for extending the blockades is to endanger our students as well as public employees. It is irresponsible."The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.On Monday, France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned any escalation in the student protests would be "irresponsible" following the arrest of 164 people.Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."The continuing student demonstrations on Tuesday coincided with nationwide walkouts by unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions. Nuñez said these protests, with at least 200,000 participants reported, mostly went without incident.

schema.headline: More than 400 detained as France student protests escalate

title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
description: Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how
body: Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning."Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.

schema.headline: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons

title: Somali pirates killed tanker crew before rescue, Puntland official tells BBC
description: Five crew members of an oil tanker seized by pirates off the coast of Somalia were killed before local security forces retook the vessel, a senior reg
body: Five crew members of an oil tanker seized by pirates off the coast of Somalia were killed before local security forces retook the vessel, a senior regional official has told the BBC.Puntland Deputy Information Minister Bile Qabowsade said the five were killed by pirates before regional forces boarded MT Hoarner 25.He said the dead included three Pakistani nationals, one Indian and one national of Myanmar. Four other crew members were injured, including three Pakistanis and one Indian.The tanker, which was carrying about 18,500 barrels of oil destined for the Somali capital, Mogadishu, was seized in April by six armed men while sailing off the coast of Somalia.Sixteen suspected pirates have been arrested, while others escaped and were being pursued, officials said.Qabowsade rejected suggestions that forces from Puntland, a semi-autonomous region of Somalia, had helped some of the pirates escape. The authorities have not given further details how the five crew members were killed or how the pirates took control of the vessel.The hijacked tanker was anchored near the Somali coast between the fishing towns of Xaafun and Bander Beyla.In April, officials had said there were 17 crew members on board when the vessel was hijacked. They included 10 Pakistanis, four Indonesians, one Indian, one Sri Lankan and a Myanmar national.Piracy off the Somali coast fell sharply after 2011 following international naval operations, but attacks and hijackings have increased again in recent years.

schema.headline: Somali pirates killed tanker crew before rescue, Puntland official tells BBC

title: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner
description: A brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of siz
body: A brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing". Backpack's wideness narrowly defeated a bear known only as 910, earning 103,344 votes to 910's 98,253 in the final round of the competition, which is run by the Katmai National Park in Alaska. The National Parks Service thanked the 16 bears who "involuntarily participated" in the competition, now in its thirteenth year. Backpack, who was described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months.His mother Holly was the 2019 Fat Bear Week winner. Backpack's name derives not from what another supporter described as the "light bulb shape" of his body, but his habit, as a cub, of climbing onto Holly's back when she waded through the park's salmon-filled Brooks River. Another supporter described him as being a "big fuzzy boy". But Backpack was not without his detractors. One person said she felt that Bear 910, a female who raised both her biological cub and an adopted niece, was a "larger bear all around. Backpack just has a bigger booty". "I just feel like 910 really put in the work this year," another 910 fan wrote on the park's Facebook page, while a voter commented, "She round, she thick my girl 910 got my vote."

schema.headline: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner

title: Fatima Zahra El Mansouri named as Morocco's first female prime minister
description: At a victory press conference, prior to her announcement as prime minister, El Mansouri was asked whether the state would need to make changes to acco
body: At a victory press conference, prior to her announcement as prime minister, El Mansouri was asked whether the state would need to make changes to accommodate her in Muslim religious ceremonies attended by the king, including Friday and Eid prayers, where men and women pray in separate sections.She did not directly answer the question, instead praising the king as "the biggest advocate for women" in the country."His Majesty is the holder of wisdom… If I am entrusted with the responsibility of head of government, it will be a great honour," she said.El Mansouri is one of Morocco's most prominent female politicians.A lawyer by training, she studied at Mohammed V University in the capital, Rabat, before continuing her education in France and the US, specialising in business and corporate law.She entered politics after Pam was founded in 2008 and became the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh in 2009. She returned to the post after the 2021 elections.In the past five years, she served as a minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under former Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.In February 2024, she became the co-ordinator of Pam's leadership coalition.El Mansouri has rejected her portrayal as an "iron woman", telling Pam's magazine in 2021: "I am neither a woman of steel nor iron... I am a free activist."During her political career, El Mansouri has rarely spoken publicly about women's rights or gender inequality, despite ongoing debates in Morocco over issues such as whether polygamy should be banned and whether men and women should have equal inheritance rights.Under Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the party that comes first in elections to the House of Representatives.Pam has been led by a collective leadership since February 2024, rather than a single secretary general.After the results were announced last week, El Mansouri said the decision was ultimately up to the king to choose between her and Lekjaa.In the past, the appointment was largely a formality, as most Moroccan parties were led by a single secretary general, making it clear who would be nominated to head the government.With 97 seats, Pam does not have a majority and will need to form a coalition to reach the 198 seats required for an absolute majority in the 395-member parliament.It is not clear which party it will work with as it has fallen out with the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which led the outgoing government in which Pam was a junior partner.The Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) ⁠rebounded with 54 seats, from only 13 in the previous election - buoyed by the return of party leader Abdelilah Benkirane, a former prime minister. After the vote, Benkirane said the party would stay in opposition, refusing a partnership with Pam.

schema.headline: Fatima Zahra El Mansouri named as Morocco's first female prime minister

title: Ekurhuleni killings: South Africa's President Ramaphosa orders crackdown on unsafe streets to keep women safe
description: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has announced an audit of unsafe streets "that place women at risk", after the bodies of 12 women were found i
body: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has announced an audit of unsafe streets "that place women at risk", after the bodies of 12 women were found in just two months east of Johannesburg.The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in a country that has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.Ramaphosa also announced plans to reduce alcohol-related violence as part of his multidisciplinary, national emergency response to the murders.He said gender-based violence could not "be accepted as a normal part of life" and admitted that South Africa had "not done enough" to protect women and girls."There has understandably been widespread fear that the discovery of these women in close proximity could indicate the work of a single perpetrator," Ramaphosa said in an address to the nation on Tuesday evening."At present, the police have not found evidence establishing that these killings were committed by a single perpetrator."Four arrests have been made so far.Admitting the government has not done enough in recent years to prevent gender-based violence, he announced a new wave of measures to help protect women and girls."Every municipality must begin a women's safety audit without delay," he said. "High-risk areas must be identified" and addressed."These audits must identify broken streetlights, overgrown public spaces, abandoned buildings, unsafe transport routes and facilities, poorly secured parks, and other conditions that place women at risk."Ramaphosa has also instructed ministers to draw up a plan for an "enforcement package" to reduce alcohol-related violence."Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator," he said."But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence, and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort."The South African president also said a deeper change, beyond policing and legislation, must take place to reduce violence against women and girls, saying it "does not begin when a fist is raised" or when a woman is raped or murdered."It begins much earlier," he said. "It begins in attitudes that regard women as inferior… with the belief that a man has the right to control a woman."It begins when jealousy is mistaken for love, when control is mistaken for protection and coercion is mistaken for affection."It begins when a man refuses to accept the word no."He went on to call on men and boys to take the lead in ending gender-based violence."We have placed the burden of male violence on women," Ramaphosa said. "That must change.""The solution to violence against women cannot be to make women less free."South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said recently that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year.

schema.headline: Ekurhuleni killings: South Africa's President Ramaphosa orders crackdown on unsafe streets to keep women safe

title: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Trump met top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AIByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 6 hour
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Trump met top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AIByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 6 hours agoUS President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.1. AI 'self-regulation' pactTrump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang."It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on TuesdayTrump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord.Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said."The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight over the technology.On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.2. Doubling down on data centresTrump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the US over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on communities.Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.The president previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".Huang, whose company produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.3. It's now 'Super Intelligence' Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said."As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.Image source, EPAImage caption, Trump spoke to the media alongside tech executives after the summitDuring an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

schema.headline: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit

title: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail
description: US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy.In an
body: US journalist Evan Gershkovich has said that he knew he was being set up by Russia when he was arrested by FSB agents and accused of being a spy.In an interview with Radio 4's Today programme, Gershkovich spoke about the moment he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in 2023, and detained him."I'm not interrogated, I'm not tortured… I'm accused of espionage," he said, describing a sense of relief: "They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage - a pawn in a greater game".Gershkovich, now 34, was sentenced to 16 years in prison, but freed 16 months later as part of a high-profile prisoner swap deal.Gershkovich had been living in Russia since 2017, and was the Wall Street Journal's foreign correspondent in Moscow when he was arrested - he is now based in Berlin, Germany. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false.On the day he was arrested, Gershkovich was in Yekaterinburg - about 1,600km (1,000 miles) east of Moscow - meeting someone who he thought was a source for a story.They were sitting in a half-empty dining hall "and a group of about half-dozen masked men marched in and said 'I think we booked that table'." An odd phrase, Gershkovich said, but on reflection it is clever because it "freezes you in place". The two men stood up and Gershkovich was told he was under arrest by the notorious and powerful FSB, Russia's domestic security service."It's at that moment that you realise it's something really serious… When it's the FSB, you know it's been planned."What about the man he'd been meeting? Gershkovich saw him disappear into the crowd.Not long after his arrest, the journalist said he realised that the fact he was not being interrogated or tortured - common tactics used by Russia's security service on spies - likely meant that he was being treated more like a commodity, not a true enemy of the state."I have this odd moment - a sense of relief flooding over me," he said. "I realised they're not treating me like a real spy. They've set me up and fabricated this case so that I can be a valuable hostage, a pawn in a greater game. That means it will take a while, but I won't be here for 12-20 years."That realisation helped him stay "stable and disciplined in prison", but also gave him a unique way of predicting what might happen next - and one guess was a prisoner swap."I assumed that it would be really loud, that it would cause a global uproar. I mean, it's a foreign correspondent for the Wall Street Journal," he said - and he was right. Media organisations around the world reported on the case, his face was on a billboard in Times Square and then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.The journalist believed that this was all part of Moscow's plan - to have a high-profile prisoner that it could swap for one of its own - and that was Vadim Krasikov, an assassin who was serving a life sentence in Germany."They [Moscow] got away with it in the sense that there were no sanctions imposed. And so they played it really smart, if you think about it cynically."Gershkovich was held in Moscow's infamous Lefortovo jail, which has held some of the country's most high-profile inmates over the years, including political prisoners and dissidents. During the Great Terror of Joseph Stalin in the 1930s, torture and execution were commonplace. He described it as a "really isolating experience", in a tiny space."That wears on you psychologically," Gershkovich said, but added that he was treated ok: "I was allowed to sleep, the food was fine."Pictures of Gershkovich smiling at cameras during his court appearances in Moscow were broadcast around the world - and that was deliberate, he said - a way of showing that he was alright."I wanted to show people this kind of defiance... We know that this is a fabricated case, and so if this is a game of theatre, let's not let [Moscow] have it play out the way they want it to."But he stressed that not everyone's time in a Russian prison is like his: "Some people... get tortured. They get broken as human beings, deprived of food, of hot water for showers, told that they're never going to see their families again. I was treated completely differently."Gershkovich compared his experience to the case of Ukrainian journalist Viktoriia Roshchyna, who died while in Russian captivity in 2024, aged 27. Months later, when her body was finally returned, it reportedly showed signs of torture and her organs had been removed.Gershkovich knew there was a prisoner swap planned three weeks before it happened - an "excruciating" time, he said, "because now every day is painfully long".When it finally did happen, on 1 August 2024, it was a moment of "pure joy". But then "the joy fades, the adrenaline subsides, and you're faced with the reality of having to return to normal life again."Gershkovich said this period was difficult and sometimes overwhelming. He wasn't sleeping, suffered panic attacks in large crowds and had a short temper because he was trying to hold in his emotions.He has seen therapists who specialise in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and said writing a book on his ordeal also helped.And what about a return to Russia? Gershkovich has a deep history with the country - his parents moved to the US from the Soviet Union in the 1970s. He grew up in a Russian-speaking home, with a Russian name, moved there when he was 25 and made many friends, including his Russian girlfriend."I would hope to get back one day, but I guess we'll have to see what comes after [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. And it's not completely clear that the next government will be any better."

schema.headline: 'I was lured into a trap': Evan Gershkovich on moment that led to 16 months in Russian jail

title: Stuck between superpowers: How Australia navigates the China-US rivalry
description: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalryImage source, ReutersImage caption, China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 202
body: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalryImage source, ReutersImage caption, China's Xi Jingping and Australia's Anthony Albanese in 2024. Relations between the two countries have been rocky in recent yearsByKaty WatsonAustralia correspondent Reporting fromTownsville, North QueenslandSnipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead.Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two.  This is a show of military might." We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan. "Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important."War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation.With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower.But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner.Image source, BBC: Katy WatsonImage caption, Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan says Australia is rehearsing for "the worst type of war"It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight."We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is.Binding tighter to the USThe war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific."We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says.And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500.A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing."Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said. "China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects."The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers.But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties.The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer.Image source, BBC: Katy WatsonImage caption, The Southern Jackaroo exercises are aimed at improving defence cooperation in the Indo-PacificBut that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US."Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll. "Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States."The 'frenemy'While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China.Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner.Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer.Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015.The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs.And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up.A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years.Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges.In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, China is Australia's biggest export marketEven with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary."There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments,"  says Lyons-Jones.This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US.Rise and fall of superpowersEarlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be".Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing."The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says.Image source, PMO AustraliaImage caption, US President Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese. Australians have cooled on their relationship with the US under TrumpBut old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one."This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang.And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act."There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says. "It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

schema.headline: Stuck between superpowers: How Australia navigates the China-US rivalry

title: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
description: Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it h
body: Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city."Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says.Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September."All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains.Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded."We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC.At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again.Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times.This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia. Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another.Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko.Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action."Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far."Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs.The situation, he admitted, was very difficult."It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things."Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center."In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC."This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average."If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming."The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction. Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia.Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware."We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv.There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added.Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon. Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery."Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't."EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine.But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat.His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed."This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

schema.headline: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign

title: Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's removal from flat
description: Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-
body: Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last week.Ministers met on Tuesday to discuss the proposals, which include a ban on evictions until 2030.Announcing the measures, Health Minister Mónica García said they would bring relief to more than five million people - but opposition politician Míriam Nogueras said the agreement left "small landlords out in the cold".The proposals - which have been presented in the form of two decrees - come into effect immediately, but must be approved by Congress within a month, although the government hopes to hold the vote as soon as this Friday. Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government lacks a majority in parliament and has struggled to get right-leaning parties to approve previous decrees.In April, a decree seeking to roll over rental contracts was blocked by right-leaning parties.García, of the Sumar alliance, said other measures agreed upon on Tuesday included the rolling over of contracts until 2028; stricter regulation of short-term and room rentals; and banning the purchase of housing by investment firms."It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," García said.Referencing the protests, she added: "Thanks to the mobilisations and the encampments. Without you, this would not have been possible."But Nogueras, spokeswoman for the centre-right Catalan nationalists of Junts party, said: "We all agreed that evictions - where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros - obviously need to be stopped."Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property - putting them all in the same basket - is a mistake," she told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.The minority government, which is made up of the Sánchez's ruling Socialists and junior partner the Sumar alliance, has 30 days from the decrees' publication to reach an agreement in parliament. Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez urged political parties to support the decrees after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week."Congress has the opportunity to tell Maricarmen that her suffering was worth it... and that many people will benefit from her battle", she said.But Valeria Racu, a spokeswoman for the Madrid Tenants' Union, said the battle had "only just begun", and called for more protests across Spain next weekend."We all have our eyes on the text, on the small print, to make sure this is the Maricarmen decree," added Alicia del Río, another spokeswoman for the organisation.The two decrees approved by the cabinet contain enough to at least suggest that the government has been listening carefully to the demands of the activists who have been protesting in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere in recent days. The temporary ban on evictions, the rolling over of rental contracts and the ban on investment firms - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property are all the kinds of policies that have been discussed by housing activists in recent days.Pablo Bustinduy, minister of social rights, described the measures approved by the cabinet as "a first step towards the economic and social transformation of the country".Bustinduy and his Sumar alliance had entered the negotiations with Sánchez's Socialists determined to take a stand on this issue, which is one they feel strongly about. Sumar's tough stance was a major reason why talks between the coalition partners on the decrees went down to the wire ahead of Tuesday's cabinet meeting.While the relatively bold new measures may please many on the left, they have raised the hackles of the Junts, whose support is again likely to be needed to approve them. Junts and other parties on the right tend to be reluctant to intervene in the housing market, particularly if it means tipping the balance of the law in favour of tenants and against landlords, many of who are their natural electorate.The question now is whether the social momentum generated by the Maricarmen Abascal case will override such reservations and manage to ensure this package of measures becomes law.Ahead of the government's announcement on Tuesday, the lawyer for Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing crisis, said she would be allowed to return to her home after reaching a deal with the company that owns it on Monday.Abascal, who was admitted to hospital after being forcibly removed from the apartment on a stretcher, was unable to attend the meeting and is yet to sign the deal.Abascal's father first rented the flat in 1956 and she had continued to live in it after her parents died, with a cap on the rent, until investment company Urbagestión bought the property in 2018. It raised the monthly rent to more than her monthly pension, leaving her unable to pay it.Abascal's case is not unique.In the north-eastern city of Zaragoza, another woman's eviction was temporarily suspended on Tuesday, the European Pressphoto Agency reported. Esmeralda Tejero, 51, has lived in a flat in the city for eight years with her 11-year-old daughter, but stopped paying her rent some time ago as she could not afford it on top of her daily living costs, she told Catalan newspaper el Periódico on Monday.Protests calling for housing relief measures broke out last week in Madrid and have spread to other cities including Barcelona, Seville, Malaga and Cadiz.Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday demanding stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.Hundreds of tents have been set up in the famous public square of Puerta del Sol since.

schema.headline: Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's removal from flat

title: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home
description: Figure caption, Watch: Videos show the al-Tubasi family's homes on fire and damage inside one of them before it was set ablazeByYolande KnellMiddle Ea
body: Figure caption, Watch: Videos show the al-Tubasi family's homes on fire and damage inside one of them before it was set ablazeByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalemMore than 100 Israeli settlers have carried out attacks in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank, stopping a family escorted by the Israeli military from returning to their homes, which had been seized weeks ago by settlers.Two houses belonging to the al-Tubasi family in Jalud, south of Nablus, were set on fire in the raid on Monday night and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers. Human rights groups say the events show how Israeli authorities are failing to take effective action against settler violence."It was extremely terrifying, beyond words. It's hard to imagine the situation," Mahmoud al-Tubasi told the BBC."My feeling now is that I am happy to have escaped death. I genuinely expected they were going to kill us."Al-Tubasi, 60, his wife Aida, 51, and their 33-year-old son, Wael, had returned to their properties accompanied by Israeli forces after Israel's High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed to go back.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Mahmoud al-Tubasi said he thought settlers were going to kill him and his familyThe family was forced to leave this summer after weeks of settler harassment and attacks.  Extremist settlers had set up an illegal outpost close to Jalud and besieged three houses, including two belonging to the al-Tubasis' sons  who are married with young daughters.Al-Tubasi said that he was called at about midnight and told that there was coordination with Israel's military for his family to go back to their houses. He received a message from Israeli officials saying that if he wanted to reclaim his property he had to go immediately with the army and Israeli border police.By torchlight, the family inspected one home.  A video shared with the BBC shows that the settlers had already extensively damaged it - smashing holes through doors, tearing out electrical fittings, ripping up tiles, breaking windows and leaving rubbish strewn about.  The toilet was smashed and appeared to be full of human waste.A large number of extremist settlers arrived in Jalud after alerts were posted in WhatsApp groups they use to coordinate action, saying that the Palestinian family they had forced out was returning and should be stopped."As soon as we entered the house, which had already been completely destroyed, settlers started throwing stones at us. The army responded by firing tear gas at them, but there were so many settlers, more than 150, that the army could no longer control them," al-Tubasi told the BBC.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Israel's High Court has ruled that the al-Tubasi family must be allowed to return to their homesThe grandfather says that a group of Israeli soldiers protected his family from the settlers who tried to approach them, using pepper spray to force them back.  Settlers slashed the tyres of a military van they were put in and then they were transferred to an armoured military vehicle.  As the family was being driven away, the settlers set fire to their car and both of their houses.  Video shot from a distance shows smoke billowing from them.Al-Tubasi says that the Israeli security forces "essentially formed a barrier, took us out safely and got us away from there. But they did not take any action against the settlers themselves."An Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said that "more than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire, and throwing stones at security forces." The Israeli military said that three police officers were lightly injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged. It described the Tubasi family as victims of "nationalist crime" adding that "due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed."The head of the local council in Jalud told reporters that residents had confronted the settlers leading to clashes which even spread to a nearby village, where a Palestinian woman was assaulted by settlers and her house set ablaze.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Israel's prime minister called on law enforcement authorities to prosecute those he called "rioters"One month ago, Aida al-Tubasi was attacked by masked Israeli settlers and injured along with American journalists who were interviewing her in Jalud.The high court decision, which criticised Israeli authorities for failing to crack down on settler violence, ruled that the family should be safely returned home by 20 September - more than a week ago.The legal ruling was strongly worded describing Israeli settlers' actions as "a completely unacceptable phenomenon that stands in contrast to the basic values and moral principles of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state."Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he strongly condemned the attacks on security forces, calling on law enforcement, "to prosecute the rioters to the fullest extent of the law." Israeli police said that they had arrested three people suspected of being involved in the attacks.Speaking at the UN General Assembly last week, Netanyahu dismissed international concerns about settler violence.  He accused the media of ignoring attacks on Jewish Israelis and covering "a handful of juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires."According to the Israeli human rights group, Yesh Din, fewer than three per cent of police investigations into settler violence over the last two decades have led to a conviction. Ziv Stahl, its executive director, said the lack of effective law enforcement was because, "the violence is part of a systematic government policy aimed at pushing Palestinians out of the area and expanding Israeli control over land in the West Bank".Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank claiming biblical and legal rights to the land. Some ministers have said they aim to "bury the idea" that an independent Palestinian state could be set up in the territory along with East Jerusalem and Gaza. Settlements and outposts are illegal under international law.Levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high this year, according to the United Nations, which says that since 2023, more than 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks and access restrictions in the occupied West Bank.In the same time period, the UN's Humanitarian Office (OCHA) has logged 6,199 attacks by Israeli settlers causing casualties or damage, external.According to OCHA, at least 82 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank this year and four Israelis have been killed - members of the security forces and civilians.  At least 23 Palestinians were killed in the context of settler attacks.

schema.headline: Israeli settlers attack West Bank village and block Palestinian family's return home

title: Aliko Dangote to launch Kenya oil refinery amid land protest in Lamu
description: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto are set to break ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's nort
body: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto are set to break ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast.Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity. Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery.Speaking to the BBC, Dangote, who is Africa's richest man, dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned.The refinery is set to become the only one in East Africa and is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway.In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available."To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests.Walid Ali, the co-founder of the Save Lamu campaign group, told the BBC that they are concerned about the environmental impact the project could have on the local community."We are asking for the findings from the environmental impact assessment so that we can see what mitigation measures are being proposed," Ali said. "This is not the first project where we have seen environmental concerns being overlooked," he added.Ali said that they were yet to raise concerns directly with the company because "they have not even engaged with the local community.""They have only been talking to the government. There is no ownership of the project by the community," he said.At the height of construction, Dangote said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project. "Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said.Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline. But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region. "Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said.Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example. "Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said.The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant. Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally.He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand.In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area."The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said.Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump.The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria, with construction due to begin on 1 November. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day. Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1bn earlier this month.

schema.headline: Aliko Dangote to launch Kenya oil refinery amid land protest in Lamu

title: 'He will never walk free’: Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
description: An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of
body: An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India.Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274).At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage"."When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor."Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added.Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth"."The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again."The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again."Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage".Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims.It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him.Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money.Tensions in Indian state after 11-year-old raped and murderedThe child abuse survivor fighting to save othersIndia media storm over 10-year-old pregnant rape victimThe emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge.Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven.The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external. And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities.Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life.In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child.After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

schema.headline: 'He will never walk free’: Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
